articles.title: German boat dealer suspected of supplying Channel smuggling gangs, BBC finds
articles.author: Jessica Parker; Tom Beal
articles.body_markdown:
**A German boat dealer is suspected by European authorities of being a key supplier to migrant smugglers operating in the English Channel, the BBC can reveal.**

Nearly a third of small-boat crossings in the first four months of this year allegedly involved boats or engines from MaReBoote, a small firm in western Germany, according to files we have seen.

The managing director, Marvin Reuter, is contesting extradition to France, where he could face smuggling, criminal conspiracy and involuntary manslaughter charges.

His equipment is suspected of being linked to two fatal accidents, in which four men died.

We confronted the 35-year-old at his business near Dortmund, but he would not answer our questions. He said he was reporting us to the police.

Reuter cannot be formally charged until extradited to France but could face jail time, if tried and convicted. He is presumed innocent until proven guilty.

The BBC - alongside German broadcasters WDR and NDR, newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung (SZ) - and France's Le Monde newspaper - has obtained and reviewed hundreds of police, court and tax documents about the case. We have blurred images of Reuter because of German privacy rules.

Investigators, we have learned, believe they have uncovered clear, persistent links between Reuter and smuggling networks.

Evidence has been gathered through the confessions of alleged accomplices and covert jail-cell recordings of an alleged gang chief - as well as the two deadly crossing attempts.

At least 82 boats from Reuter's firm reached the English coast in just over two years to May, according to French investigations.

There are also press photos dating back five years showing the MaReBoote logo on dinghies crowded with migrants.

In 2021, Reuter told the Sun and Guardian he felt "frustrated" and "anxious" that his vessels had ended up in the hands of smugglers.

There was no suggestion, at that time, that authorities suspected him of wrongdoing as a German detective reportedly told the Sun: "This would be like if somebody buys a Mercedes and does something in another country which is wrong. The Mercedes seller can't help that."

It is not exactly clear when police suspicions were aroused.

French prosecutor Samuel Finielz would not comment on the details of the investigation but confirmed the head of a German company is currently the subject of a European Arrest Warrant.

The warrant was issued in May this year and relates to alleged offences dating back to December 2024.

While selling boats is "perfectly legal" it becomes illegal, said Finielz, "when one is fully aware that they will be used by networks involved in illegal immigration or human trafficking".

Case files we have seen say that German police had learned from UK authorities that 29% of detected crossings this year, up to the end of April, involved boats and/or engines linked to MaReBoote.

In France, five other men have already been charged as part of the investigation - an Iranian, three Iraqis and a Syrian.

In one of the two fatal incidents where Reuter's equipment is suspected to be involved, one of those who died was also Syrian.

Suliman al Husein would have just turned 20 when he died, according to a birth date listed in the files.

News reports at the time say he suffered a cardiac arrest after likely being crushed on a packed dinghy during a failed launch, west of Calais, in January 2025.

He was the first migrant to die in the English Channel that year. His body was found on the floor of the boat which, investigators allege, bore the MaReBoote logo.

The case against Reuter also stems from a chance arrest when French police pulled over a vehicle with German plates, near the northern port city of Boulogne-sur-Mer.

The BMW, which was towing a trailer, was spotted overtaking another vehicle at speed in the early hours of a morning in May this year - police records say.

Inside the car were two German nationals who - according to a subsequent search - were transporting jerry cans of fuel, a boat engine, pumps and a rolled up inflatable dinghy.

The men claimed they had been paid up to â¬1,000-a-time (Â£830) to make several, similar drops to "foreigners" on the coast, interrogation records show.

"Of course I knew that it wasn't legal," one is said to have admitted under questioning. "The money made me turn a blind eye."

Both men, who have since been convicted for smuggling offences, allegedly implicated Marvin Reuter as the man who had hired and paid them for this work.

Police files say both the BMW and the boat it was carrying had MaReBoote logos on them.

Marvin Reuter was arrested in Germany in May and later released, pending extradition.

On the day of his arrest, German police also seized more than 30 dinghies and 9,000 life jackets. Equipment which, we can now reveal, was allegedly linked to Reuter.

The BBC was previously granted access to see this haul, held in a police warehouse at a secret location in western Germany.

Meanwhile, further evidence has been gleaned from the bugging of a jail cell of a suspected gang chief, who is being held in pre-trial detention in France.

Recordings captured the inmate talking about buying nautical equipment from a German firm run by a man with Reuter's first name: Marvin - according to files we have seen.

The MaReBoote company address was also discovered on the alleged smuggler's phone, the case files say.

When we confronted Reuter last month at his business in the town of Werne, in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia, he told us to leave and drove off.

He then returned a short time later and said he was reporting us to the police. He did not answer our questions.

We approached him in writing before and after this encounter including a detailed request for comment. In response to that request, he did not address the specific allegations but accused us of harassment.

It is understood Reuter's lawyers have challenged his extradition, citing overcrowding in French prisons as one reason. Their client should face any allegations in Germany, they argue.

In Germany, it became explicitly illegal to aid smuggling to the UK at the end of last year after a prior BBC investigation exposed the country's role as a storage hub for gangs. Before then, some anti-smuggling laws in Germany had no longer applied to the UK because of Brexit.

The raid that saw the seizure of equipment that was allegedly linked to Reuter marked the first time the new law had been used.

Small boat crossings have dropped significantly in 2026, with British authorities citing law enforcement as a "key factor". However, illegal migration into Europe has also been falling.

The UK National Crime Agency's (NCA) deputy director for organized immigration crime, Dan Cannatella-Barcroft, praised Germany's "commitment" to tackling people-smuggling but acknowledged the country would remain "an important piece of the puzzle".

While a gap in the law has been closed, Germany's proximity to France, wider transport links and the fact that some of the Kurdish-dominated gangs are based there, means it is expected to stay as a transit point in the illegal small-boats trade.

The "vast majority" of small boats equipment in the past few years has come through Germany, Cannatella-Barcroft told the BBC - much of it made in China and having been routed through Turkey.

articles.title: North Korea's Kim vows to build more nuclear weapons after ignoring Trump's overture
articles.author: The Associated Press
articles.body_markdown:
SEOUL, South Korea — North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited facilities that produce nuclear ingredients and called for building more nuclear weapons, days after ignoring U.S. President Donald Trump's offer to meet during his recent visit to Asia.

Experts say Kim likely wants to show off his evolving nuclear arsenal, the backbone of his authoritarian rule, and reaffirm his rejection of any future talks on dismantling his nuclear program.

The North's official Korean Central News Agency said Thursday that Kim inspected two nuclear materials production factories, one newly inaugurated and the other being expanded. KCNA photos showed Kim and senior military officials walking between dense rows of what appeared to be centrifuges used to produce weapons-grade uranium and touring halls displaying what were believed to be warheads. Some of the images were blurred.

KCNA said Kim visited a nuclear-powered equipment production base and a nuclear research institute as well on Wednesday.

North Korea has disclosed a uranium enrichment site a few times since it showed one at its main Yongbyon nuclear complex to visiting American scholars in 2010. North Korea didn't say where the nuclear materials production factories that Kim visited this week are located. In June, when North Korea disclosed parts of a uranium enrichment site while reporting on Kim's visit there, outside experts assessed it was likely an additional uranium enrichment facility at Yongbyon.

**Kim justifies nuke program by citing threats from US, South Korea**Kim said his latest inspection visit was part of efforts to strengthen North Korea's defense capabilities in response to "variable nuclear threats approaching the Korean Peninsula moment by moment." He accused the U.S. of inciting its regional allies to possess nuclear-powered submarines and committing to sharing its nuclear weapons with them, KCNA said.

"The validity and substantiality of our possession of nuclear weapons and the trend of bolstering up its nuclear capability in quality and quantity are an irreversible reality," Kim said, according to KCNA.

Kim also said the deployment of low-yield battlefield nuclear weapons across multiple domains for various missions is crucial and urgent given North Korea's "inevitable reality facing the border with the most dangerous enemy state," a reference to South Korea. North Korea has in recent years focused on developing such tactical nuclear weapons amid heightened animosity with South Korea.

"Trump has talked about a willingness to meet Kim Jong Un, but the basic U.S. position that North Korea must denuclearize remains unchanged. So Kim Jong Un wants to say 'Look at how powerful we are. Don't talk about denuclearization if you want to meet us,'" said Moon Seong Mook, an analyst for the Seoul-based Korea Research Institute for National Strategy.

Moon said Kim's visit to the nuclear facilities was also likely meant to check on how state objectives on the nuclear program have progressed this year and what future goals must be set ahead of a year-end Workers' Party conference.

South Korea's Defense Ministry said it takes Kim's comments on battlefield nuclear weapons seriously and added that Seoul maintains a firm military readiness against Pyongyang's nuclear threats under an alliance with the U.S. South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff declined to share an analysis of the North Korean nuclear facilities reported by KCNA, calling it confidential information for South Korea and the U.S.

**Trump still hopes to meet Kim**Trump reiterated his eagerness to restore diplomacy with Kim as he visited China last week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. But a Trump-Kim meeting didn't happen, with Pyongyang not publicly responding to Trump's overture.

In an interview with the New York Post this week, Trump dismissed the suggestion that Kim had rebuffed his outreach, saying, "No, he didn't ignore it. You know, we had many leaders there … There'll be a time when we meet … It was just not really the right time. It was a very busy two-day period."

Trump also claimed he could revive diplomacy with Kim at any time by restarting the exchange of letters they maintained during his first term, although he acknowledged that the two leaders had not corresponded "recently."

Kim has previously said he could return to talks if the U.S. drops its "hostile policy" against his country and respects what he calls the North's status as a nuclear state. Experts say Kim aims to win international recognition as a nuclear state so that he could demand the lifting of international sanctions.

Last week, International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Grossi assessed North Korea has been expanding its original uranium enrichment facility at Yongbyon, calling the move "a cause for serious concern."

Nuclear weapons can be built using either highly enriched uranium or weapons-grade plutonium, and North Korea has facilities to produce both at Yongbyon. Last year, South Korea's Unification Minister Chung Dong-young said that North Korea was operating four uranium enrichment facilities and that they were running every day.

articles.title: What Makes Up the Cosmos? A 20-Year Survey Hints That Something Is Missing.
articles.author: Charlie Wood
articles.body_markdown:
Dark Energy Survey/DOE/FNAL/

DECam/CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA

Joshua Frieman remembers when the world found out that the universe was made of much more than just matter. For a few years, the scientist had been studying the possibility that the cosmos needed something else — a “missing energy” — to make sense. But it was a niche idea. When he and a colleague started to plan a workshop on the topic in 1997, at first only a few dozen people signed up. Then, in early 1998, two teams of researchers announced that exploding stars called supernovas seemed to be racing away from Earth under the influence of an unidentified, omnipresent repellent force. The observations implied the existence of exactly the sort of missing energy that Frieman and his colleagues planned to talk about.

“Suddenly, everyone wanted to come to our workshop,” including reporters with TV cameras, said Frieman, who was then at the University of Chicago. It was “kind of a circus.”

Within a few years, cosmologists had arrived at a whole new view of reality. The missing energy, given the name “dark energy” for its invisible nature, was pushing galaxies apart. The energy seemed embedded in space itself. It made up roughly two-thirds of creation (with matter — visible and dark — making up the remainder). Frieman embarked on what would become a two-decade mission to learn about dark energy by watching how it influences all that we can see: the Dark Energy Survey (DES).

Now that project has come to a close. In May 2026, DES shared findings based on its full dataset of thousands of supernovas and hundreds of millions of galaxies spanning billions of years of cosmic history. Those findings, in combination with data gathered by a different project, the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), suggest that our understanding of what the universe is made of — the venerable “standard model” of cosmology — is not complete. “There appear to be cracks in that model,” said Simone Ferraro, a cosmologist at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. “There’s something that doesn’t fit.”

Brian Nord

Cosmologists can’t yet say what that something is. What they can say is that after 20 years of stability, their field is returning to a state of confusion. “It’s certainly enough to make you either uncomfortable or excited,” Ferraro said.

## **Bigger and Faster Forever**

Experimental cosmology is a piecemeal endeavor. It’s a bit like trying to reconstruct a person’s life from a dossier of data about them: report cards, utility bills, cholesterol tests, and so on. You come up with a story that weaves all the data together, go find new data, and use it to refine the story. Frieman and other cosmologists started to speculate about a missing form of energy in the mid-1990s because the story they were telling didn’t seem quite right.

In previous decades, they had peered at the sky and inferred roughly how much stuff was out there. They saw a smattering of galaxies lighting up the void — visible matter. Based on how fast the galaxies were spinning, astronomers deduced that a preponderance of invisible matter must surround each bright speck, holding it together — dark matter.

The rate at which these galaxies were receding from view implied that the universe had been expanding for some 8 billion to 13 billion years. It looked as if there was just enough matter (dark and visible combined) to tug gravitationally on the universe and continuously slow this expansion without ever bringing it to a full halt.

But new observations started to clash with this accounting. Astronomers spotted stars, for instance, that seemed to be older than the universe. While trying to understand these and other anomalies, cosmologists noticed that it helped to add a new type of energy to their models.

Then came the bombshell 1998 findings that the expansion of the universe was not actually slowing down; it was ever so slightly speeding up. By the end of the year, the unknown stuff driving that acceleration had a name: dark energy. Frieman charged off to measure it.

In 1998, cosmologists were like detectives with a thin dossier. They had a blurry image of light from the early universe known as the cosmic microwave background (CMB). And they had observed several million galaxies, along with dozens of supernovas. Because light takes time to travel, these observations gave cosmologists snapshots of what the universe looked like at different moments over the past few billion years.

DOE/FNAL/DECam/R. Hahn/CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA

That was just enough data to show that the universe was experiencing an unexpected growth spurt. But to figure out exactly when it had started and how fast it was happening, Frieman and his colleagues would need to fatten their file. Their solution was DES.

DES began in 2003, with a handful of physicists at Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory brainstorming what it would take to get a more comprehensive view of the cosmos. They went on to design and build the 570-megapixel Dark Energy Camera, the most powerful digital camera of its era, and install it on the 4-meter-wide Blanco telescope in the Chilean Andes. They then used it to conduct the Dark Energy Survey, which ran for 758 nights between 2013 and 2019. During this time, DES increased the number of recorded galaxies to hundreds of millions. DES was supposed to end in 2018, but the researchers extended it to make up for lousy observations due to clouds from a strong El Niño season.

Every couple of years the DES collaboration, which grew to include more than 400 scientists across seven countries, would analyze the data they had collected so far to see what it suggested about the history of our universe. Again and again, what they found was consistent with the theory that had coalesced after the 1998 supernova papers: The universe was about 30% matter (mostly an invisible and lethargically drifting “cold dark matter,” or CDM), and the remaining 70% of the universe was dark energy. Physicists noted that this energy acted like an unchanging property of the vacuum of space, referred to as “lambda.” The bigger space gets, the more of this vacuum energy there is, and the faster the cosmos expands. This theory of the universe became known as Lambda-CDM.

Then, in 2024, researchers from a next-generation experiment, DESI, combined the DES observations with a sharper image of the CMB and new observations of their own. They found that the Lambda-CDM theory no longer quite fit.

## **Broken Record**

Whereas DES uses one big camera in Chile, DESI at Kitt Peak in Arizona uses thousands of tiny eyes. Each can swivel to focus on a single galaxy. The individualized attention more precisely captures each galaxy’s motion.

This technology lets DESI see hidden cosmic structures. Due to the way that sound waves rippled through matter in the early universe, spherical shells of slightly dense matter formed. Over time, matter in these shells gathered into galaxies. Each shell is the same size, so by looking at how big or small it appears from Earth, scientists can tell how far away its galaxies are.

Combining the distances to the galaxies with other observations, the researchers can calculate how fast the universe has grown over the past 10 billion years or so (out of the 13.8 billion years since the Big Bang).

Dark Energy Survey/DOE/FNAL/

DECam/CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA

In 2024, the DESI collaboration dropped a bombshell report. When researchers added their shells to the existing dossier, they couldn’t get the Lambda-CDM model to fit all the data. What fit better was an exotic theory that replaced lambda, the constant vacuum energy, with a different form of energy that weakened over time. A year later, an analysis of more data found the same thing.

In the meantime, the DES collaboration continued to analyze the galaxies they had photographed. Those researchers focused on building a different contribution to the dossier: a detailed record of a cosmic tug-of-war.

While gravity pulls matter — mostly dark matter — together, dark energy fights back, pushing matter apart. By measuring how much matter has clumped together in different eras, cosmologists can infer the strength of dark energy over time.

DES assesses this clumping in different ways, explained Sujeong Lee, a physicist at Ohio University. The visible part of each galaxy marks the heart of a vast cloud of dark matter. DES measures how tightly these dark matter clouds cluster together by looking at the clustering of visible matter at their centers. It also looks at the way that dark matter influences the light coming from distant galaxies in the background, allowing scientists to reconstruct a precise map of the matter in the universe.

Each of these measurements involves comparing pair after pair of DES’s hundreds of millions of galaxies, looking for tiny distortions in their positions and shapes. After seven years of rigorous analysis, the collaboration published their final results in early 2026. “It’s been a real tour de force,” said Ferraro, who isn’t part of DES. “It pushed the analysis to a new level.”

Alongside these measurements, DES also reprocessed a catalog they had compiled of 1,600 recently observed supernovas, establishing the sharpest view yet of the modern universe. “I trust the DES-reanalyzed supernova data much more than I trust any other supernova dataset,” said Seshadri Nadathur, a DESI cosmologist, in the spring. (Since then, other teams have re-analyzed their supernova catalogs, and all leading catalogs align closely).

Cosmologists have now assembled their thickest file on the universe to date. DES merged its map of matter clumping, its supernova catalog, DESI’s galaxy shells, and a CMB image, then checked to see how well Lambda-CDM could still account for the whole cosmic history.

The answer: not very well. In their final report, DES scientists found that their data fit somewhat better with the theory that dark energy is not stable and has slackened in recent eons. In the statistical language of physicists, DES reports a “three-sigma” preference for the new theory. That’s significant enough to make people pay attention, especially since it combines data collected in different ways, but it falls far short of the “five-sigma” confidence physicists need to claim a new discovery.

CTIO/NOIRLab/DOE/NSF/AURA/R. Hahn (Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory)

Adding to the intrigue, DES found that the mismatch can’t be explained away if, for instance, one of the datasets holds some hidden error. If you assume Lambda-CDM is right, the CMB picture doesn’t quite match the matter maps; the matter maps don’t quite match the supernovas; and the supernovas don’t quite match the CMB picture. There is no single item that you can toss from the file to make everything fit, so no single observation looks fishier than the others.

This suggests that the tension is less likely to be a random artifact — the kind that could easily arise from the merger of millions of observations using different instruments — and is more likely to reflect a clash between the real universe and our understanding of it. “There’s something that doesn’t fit,” Ferraro said. And “we’re trying to figure out what that something is.”

## **Mystery Upon Mystery**

articles.title: How the Galileo musical’s composer sets science to a score on Broadway
articles.author: Emma Gometz
articles.body_markdown:
What must it have been like to put your eye to the first Galilean telescope? A new musical on Broadway depicts the experience as absolutely electric—with a swelling chorus and pumped-up rock sound blaring while stars shine all around the audience.

*Galileo* is a new Broadway musical opening on December 6. It tells the story of pioneering astronomer Galileo Galilei and the way that his public support for the heliocentric view of the universe sparked conflict with the Catholic Church. The show’s ballads depict how the Church hobbled Galileo’s efforts to advance astronomy, but it also makes it clear that he was both a man of faith and a rebellious soul. (The sometimes Christian rock–like melodies and lyrics also support this aspect of the character.) The show doesn’t shy away from the complications of Galileo’s conflict with the church, propelled by his close friendship with Bishop Maffeo Barberini, who later, as pope, played a key role in forcing Galileo to recant and sentencing him to house arrest for teaching heliocentrism.

*Galileo*’s music, lyrics and arrangements were created by composers Michael Weiner and Zoe Sarnak. Once it opens, Sarnak will be focusing her creative attention as composer of two more STEM (science, technology, engineering and mathematics)–themed musicals: *Particle Fever*, an adaptation of a 2013 documentary about the discovery of the Higgs boson with the same title, and a stage adaptation of the film *A Beautiful Mind.* “I’m in my science era, I like to joke,” she says. “And I’m thrilled about it.”

*Scientific American* spoke to Sarnak about how sound tells Galileo’s story in the new musical, how she puts science to a soundtrack and why this story is ripe for a retelling today.

\[*An edited transcript of the conversation follows*.\]

**You studied science before you decided to become a composer. How did your research experience fuel your music?**

I would say, if you asked kids from my high school what they thought I was going to be when I grew up, they would say a mathematician or a scientist. My dad is a mathematician, my mom studied philosophy... She does ethics of technology at Cornell Tech. I took music as something I did for fun..., because I’ve been composing music since I was very young. But I have a family of professors and doctors, so that’s sort of the family trade, you know? So I was doing molecular bio and music in parallel in my undergrad. I worked in a virology lab, and it was a huge part of my life.

I think there’s a relationship between \[molecular biology and music\] in thinking in a map-based way and integrating layers of information, as opposed to just one linear thought. When you think about music and how it works, as a composer, you're thinking melody, harmony, rhythmic structures, counterpoints, how they all come together. And I think that the puzzle that is, for example, molecular bio is kind of similar in that way.

What has been cool about this moment as I come into writing *Galileo* and *Particle Fever* is: I can actually explore the emotion behind what these scientists go through. The soul of a scientist sings to me because of the dreamer quality, because of the creative, thinking-outside-the-box quality. If *Sunday in the Park with George* makes sense as a musical, then certainly *Galileo* does.

**What drew you to Galileo’s story?**

He was this kind of rebellious figure speaking truth to power. And when \[Weiner and I\] started to talk about it, it felt useful to imagine that he’s a rock star because of that. And suddenly, you can feel how explosive he is, how brave he is, how unbridled and brash he is, which, by the way, *he was*. Like the actual Galileo was certainly not a meek man. And I remember thinking about the way \[punk musician\] Patti Smith talks about using music to speak truth to power. And it’s like, if there's a lens for this person’s story to be told, it’s through rock music.

It makes sense once you start working on something like this and you see how much people have engaged with his story through the years in various art forms because the stakes are so high and it’s evergreen in its relevance, for better or worse, because we’re constantly coming up against moments where a new way of thinking hits up against the power structure. That’s part of the ebbs and flows of how civilization works. And so that got me really excited about a way in which we could tell this story that can only be told through a musical, theatrically.

**I heard that you wanted to have each character in Galileo’s story have a distinct musical sound. Can you describe what they are and why?**

Starting with Galileo, we were really interested in a version of his sound that feels sort of \[like\] rebellious, unbridled rock. He’s pushing against a system that doesn’t want to let a new idea come into the light, and so he has to explode against it. That felt very clear. He still has a lot of depth emotionally, and we do have moments where he’s quite quiet, but those tend to be personal, with Barberini or with his daughter Virginia. But to capture the sound of what it would mean to see the \[celestial bodies\] that no one had seen..., that would be like a “hits you in your core” kind of experience. So we knew we wanted that for him.

With his daughter Virginia, then, we were thinking about how his real daughter had wisdom and soulfulness to her. She was born into a very difficult circumstance, and yet their correspondence shows that she was very brilliant as well, \[with\] an ability not to be toppled by a system that was really quite stacked against her. But she has a younger sound purposefully. We want her to start in the space of hopeful the way that teenagers are and then evolve into the version of her that is in Act II.

I think with the pope, we use a lot of strings but strings in this chamber way that sounds influenced by music in mass—a chamber classical element to the church sound. Barberini has a beauty to what he sings, but he pulls it in a modern direction. Until you get to what happens in Act II, he’s a progressive thinker within the realm of the church, which helped us shape his sound.

**Can you preview some musical choices you made for** *Particle Fever?*

*Galileo* sits at the intersection of a scientist and his dreams and the political circumstance and how those explode against one another, whereas *Particle Fever* is zoomed in. It’s set at CERN, and we’re asking people to dive into the importance of discovering the Higgs boson. It’s a whole world of physics that we have to immerse people in. Because particle physics speaks to the tiny and also, therefore, the origins of the universe—the infinite—it has a scope of pointillism up to massive orchestral gestures. And that’s really exciting, musically, for me because it lets these two shows have very different sound worlds.

I think that the shared thing is definitely the humanity that lives inside of our desire to explore and progress. For *Particle Fever,* there’s this question of whether or not those kinds of projects will be funded moving forward and whether we, as a civilization, commit to the importance of discovery. So a big part of *Particle Fever* is saying, “This is core to who we are as people.”

**Why should science stories be told on Broadway right now?**

As a composer and a writer, it’s important to make things that are beautiful, but it’s also important to know you have something to say about the world outside of your art form. And I feel honored that I have an opportunity to advocate for research, science and the progress that comes when we follow the intuition and the rigor of the human mind, things that I took for granted because of my context growing up, and now I feel it’s a duty to fight for them.

I think it is very clear that we are in a time where the questions \[are\] “What is truth? How do we advocate for progress?” Those questions are very much on my mind and all of our minds. That is why I think \[Galileo, especially\] is wildly relevant today.

articles.title: My War Against Leaf Blowers and Other Noise Crimes
articles.author: Sarah Miller
articles.body_markdown:
I live between two small business districts in a quaint little California mountain village. Sunlight streams through enormous cedars. The speed limit is a lazy twenty-five miles per hour, the poppies in the drought-resistant gardens cartoonishly bright. But if you are feeling jealous maybe you shouldn’t, because a large part of each day is ruined for me by the sound of leaf blowers. Most households near me have at least one. They are such cherished objects that I imagine them tucked up in garages and sheds inside satin-lined cribs. You might assume that tidying one’s lawn once a week would suffice, but many people seem to prefer to do it daily. There is an apartment complex across the street, and a condo complex just next to it, and, if their maintenance crews are both working at the same time of day, there might be as many as four blowers going at once, a sadistic twist on a barbershop quartet.

A few years ago, I tried to gauge my neighbors’ interest in trying to ban or greatly restrict the use of gas-powered leaf blowers. It was obvious that I was outnumbered; my frayed sanity was all the proof I needed that the neighborhood’s pro-blower contingent was strong. Still, I figured at least one or two people might share my rage that no stretch of quiet—not at dawn, not at sunset, not on Sundays—was too sacred to be blasted to smithereens in the name of landscaping.

You’d think I’d said that I wanted to get rid of pets, or running water. “How will I blow out my gutters?” one neighbor asked, his lower lip quivering. I’d seen him blow out the gutters on his roof only once. His lawn, meanwhile, looked like it belonged on a Netflix show where someone with a brand new Audi has just been murdered. The neighbors who did not use the devices seemed unbothered by the people who did. One day, I was standing in the middle of the street trying to figure out the whereabouts of what sounded like seven different leaf blowers. One of my neighbors got out of her car and, seeing my distress, said, “Aww, poor thing,” as if I were a baby who had just dropped my binky rather than one of many adult Americans being driven mad by machines that have, by the way, been banned or restricted in some two hundred cities and towns across the U.S. (These bans and restrictions are specifically on gas-powered leaf blowers; electric ones are considerably quieter, less carcinogenic, and less harmful to the environment, though I can’t say I love them either.)
